title: The Happiness Hypothesis
author: Jonathan Haidt

edition.name: Finding Modern Truth in Ancient Wisdom

thesis: Enduring maxims about living well become useful only when tested against how minds, relationships, and cultures actually work. Flourishing depends neither entirely on inner control nor entirely on external conditions, but on building a workable fit among automatic emotion, deliberate thought, social bonds, purposeful activity, and larger moral commitments.
teachingArc: The opening chapters explain the divided mind, emotional change, reciprocity, and self-serving moral judgment. The middle chapters examine the conditions of happiness, attachment, adversity, virtue, and experiences of sacredness. The final chapters join love and purposeful work into an account of meaning, then resolve the competing wisdom traditions through balance rather than a single universal formula.

signatureMoves: opens each inquiry with a maxim from an older wisdom tradition
moves from a vivid human or animal case to a named psychological mechanism
tests broad moral advice by distinguishing where it works from where it fails
uses compact metaphors such as rider and elephant to connect research findings
closes by translating evidence into a qualified practical implication
avoidMoves: does not treat any one philosophical tradition as sufficient
does not present happiness as constant positive mood
avoids giving unsupported inspiration in place of mechanisms

notes: The frozen record follows the 2006 Basic Books unabridged edition (ISBN 9780465003686). The separately titled introduction is not counted among the eleven numbered chapters. Some catalogs label the final entry 'Conclusion: On Balance'; the author-maintained chapter list and Google Books render its chapter title as 'On Balance', which is used here.
